passage:
In the canteen Nilesh, a first-year, pulled out a chair. “Keerthana, you did Prof. Verma's course. Is he fair with marks?”

Keerthana set down her samosa. “Honestly, yes, from what I saw. He gives the rubric on day one and sticks to it. But he's slow to reply to emails, so ask early.”

“What about the internal exam?”

“Two people in my batch said it was hard. I only know my batch, so check with others too.”

Priya, at the end of the table, grinned. “And he wears the same tie every Monday, ha!”

Keerthana shook her head. “That's not useful, Priya. He's fair. That's what Nilesh needs to know.”

qa.q: When does Prof. Verma give the rubric?
qa.a: Prof. Verma gives the rubric on day one and sticks to it.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana add, “I only know my batch”?
qa.a: Keerthana wanted to be accurate and not present a small sample as the whole truth.

qa.q: What choice did Keerthana make when Priya joked about the tie?
qa.a: Keerthana said the joke was not useful and steered back to what Nilesh needed: that the professor is fair.

qa.q: What might Nilesh, a first-year, gain from Keerthana's answer?
qa.a: Nilesh gets practical, honest information to plan with, and may feel welcomed by a senior who took the question seriously.

grounding: A student shares talk that informs, such as a fair professor, staying accurate and refusing to turn it into cruel entertainment.

passage:
“Devika, you worked with Aarti on the lab report last term, right?” Bidisha asked. “Should I pick her as my partner?”

“Depends,” Devika said. “Aarti's smart, but she missed two of our deadlines and told us at midnight. I had to finish the graphs myself.”

“So she's unreliable?”

“I'd say she needs firm deadlines. Maybe she was unwell, I don't know. Ask her first.”

Tara, on the bench, snorted. “She also cried in the lab when she broke a flask, remember?”

Devika frowned. “That's not information, Tara, that's a story to laugh at. Bidisha's asking about deadlines.”

“Fair,” Bidisha said. “I'll ask her straight.”

qa.q: How many deadlines did Aarti miss?
qa.a: Aarti missed two of the deadlines.

qa.q: Why did Devika say, “Maybe she was unwell, I don't know”?
qa.a: Devika felt cautious about judging Aarti unfairly and wanted to share only what was accurate, without guessing the reason for the missed deadlines.

qa.q: What choice did Bidisha make at the end?
qa.a: Bidisha decided to ask Aarti straight rather than rely on the story.

qa.q: How might Aarti feel if the story about the flask were passed around?
qa.a: Aarti would probably feel embarrassed and hurt, since a moment of upset was turned into entertainment.

grounding: A student shares useful warning about a partner's missed deadlines, while separating accurate information from a story told only for laughs.

passage:
In the small college town of Sagar, Seema had lived in the girls' PG for two years. When Lavanya arrived as a new student, Seema took her for chai.
“Useful things,” Seema said. “Mr Tiwari near the bus stand keeps deposits and never returns them, three girls lost theirs. Professor Jain is strict but fair, so don't fear her. And the library closes early on Saturdays.”
Lavanya wrote it all down.
Then two other girls joined them, laughing. “Tiwari's daughter, did you see her dress at the mela? Such a show-off.”
Seema shook her head. “That's not useful. That's just mean.” She turned back to Lavanya. “The deposit thing is true. The rest, don't bother with.”

qa.q: Where does Mr Tiwari live?
qa.a: He lives near the bus stand.

qa.q: How did Seema seem to feel when the girls mocked Tiwari's daughter?
qa.a: She seemed uncomfortable and firm, not wanting useful advice turned into cruel entertainment.

qa.q: What is the difference between Seema's warning and the girls' talk?
qa.a: Seema's warning was accurate and meant to protect Lavanya's money, while the girls' talk about the dress was just for mocking.

qa.q: How might Lavanya use what Seema told her?
qa.a: Lavanya will probably avoid renting from Mr Tiwari and feel more confident with Professor Jain, while ignoring the gossip about the daughter.

grounding: Shows a student sharing accurate warnings about a landlord and a professor to protect a newcomer, while refusing cruel entertainment.

passage:
In the student kitchen in Berlin, Felix was showing the new exchange student, Rafael, how things worked.
“Professor Weber is tough, but she marks fairly. Dr Lang loses assignments, so always email him a copy. And be careful lending money to Jonas on the second floor. He's borrowed from three of us and never paid back.”
Rafael nodded. “Is he, like, a bad guy?”
Felix paused. He could have said a lot. Jonas's messy room, his weird girlfriend, the time he cried at a party. The others would have laughed.
Instead he said, “No. Just don't lend him money. That's all I know for sure.”
Later, Rafael politely refused when Jonas asked for twenty euros. Jonas shrugged and asked someone else.

qa.q: Who does Felix say loses assignments?
qa.a: Dr Lang loses assignments.

qa.q: What was Felix feeling when he paused before answering?
qa.a: He felt tempted to share juicy stories but uneasy about it, choosing to stick to what was true and useful.

qa.q: What makes Felix's warning about Jonas useful rather than cruel?
qa.a: It's accurate, limited to what Felix knows, and meant to protect Rafael, not to entertain others.

qa.q: How might Jonas be affected if Felix had shared the other stories?
qa.a: He could have been mocked and judged for private things that had nothing to do with money.

grounding: Shows a student passing on accurate, useful cautions to a newcomer while choosing not to add entertaining but cruel details.

passage:
In the college hostel, Vidya noticed first-year Jomon looking nervous outside the mess. She asked him quietly what was wrong.
“A senior, Pratik, asked me for five hundred rupees. He said juniors who don't pay get ‘trained’.”
Vidya's jaw tightened. She knew Pratik had done this before. “That's ragging. Don't pay. Come with me.” She walked him straight to the warden's office, where the warden took his complaint that evening.
Back in the common room, some seniors were already talking about Pratik. “His father's a drunk, that's why.” “His sister failed twice.”
Vidya cut in. “Stop. What he did to Jomon is the only thing that matters, and it's been reported. The rest is just cruel.”

qa.q: How much money did Pratik ask for?
qa.a: He asked for five hundred rupees.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel when Jomon told her?
qa.a: Her jaw tightened; she felt angry and protective, knowing Pratik had done this before.

qa.q: Which kind of talk about Pratik was useful, and which was not?
qa.a: Warning and reporting what he did to Jomon was useful and accurate; the talk about his father and sister was cruel entertainment.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt walking to the warden's office?
qa.a: He was likely nervous but relieved to have a senior on his side, not facing it alone.

grounding: Shows a student using accurate information to protect a first-year from ragging, while refusing cruel gossip about the senior's family.

passage:
Asif,
You start at my college next month, so here's the guide I wish I'd had.
Professor Rao looks strict but is the fairest marker in the department. If you're stuck, go to her office hours; she'll spend an hour on one doubt.
Don't lend your lab notes to Vicky in third year. He borrowed mine twice and returned them once, with tea on page six. That's not me being mean. It's what happened, and I've said it to his face.
You'll hear plenty of other stuff in the hostel: who's dating whom, whose family has money, why someone dropped a year. Most of it is rubbish and none of it helps you. When the talk goes there, I go and make tea.
My rule: if it keeps you safe or saves you time, and I know it's true, I'll tell you. If it's just for laughs, I won't.
See you on the 3rd. Bring a bucket.
Wasim bhai

qa.q: Who is the fairest marker in the department?
qa.a: Professor Rao is the fairest marker in the department.

qa.q: How does Wasim seem to feel about the hostel gossip?
qa.a: Wasim seems fed up and uncomfortable with it, preferring to go and make tea rather than join in.

qa.q: What line does Wasim draw between useful talk and cruel gossip?
qa.a: Share something only if it is true and keeps Asif safe or saves time; skip anything that's just for laughs.

qa.q: How might Vicky feel if he read what Wasim wrote?
qa.a: Vicky might feel embarrassed or annoyed, but since it's accurate and already said to his face, it reads as a fair warning, not a cruel story.

grounding: Shows a young adult passing on accurate, useful information about people to a younger cousin while refusing gossip that only entertains.
